_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Who married an Israelite … and she does not pay the fifth: for she is not a stranger [zara], since she has not been profaned: if her husband dies and she marries a priest, she eats [teruma]; or if she has no offspring, she returns to teruma.
rashi:a1.2: She pays, etc.: [the word] “guilt offering” is not part of our reading.
rashi:a2.1: And her death is by strangulation: Rabbi Meir follows his own line of reasoning, that even though at the outset she was not a stranger, now at any rate she is a stranger.
rashi:a3.1: And the Rabbis: this is Rabbi Yehuda, his [Rabbi Meir’s] disputant.
rashi:a3.2: In both this case and that case, etc.: since we require one who is a stranger from the outset.
rashi:a4.1: And by those answers that we answered: that Rabbi Meir’s reason is that [placing] is juxtaposed with applying.
rashi:a4.2: But placing in general: for example, “he shall not put frankincense on it” [Leviticus 5:11], said of the meal offering of a sinner, [is] with an olive-bulk, which we derive from “and he shall give to the priest the sacred item” (Leviticus 22:14). And so it is explained in the chapter Kol HaMenaḥot Baot Matza (Menaḥot 59b).
rashi:a5.1: It is written lo yisakh: with two letters yod. Put one of them inside the word and read lo yasikh, which means: one who is commanded not to apply [the oil], neither to himself nor to others, is the one whom another is commanded not to anoint. And a gentile is not subject to the commandment.
rashi:a6.1: A priest who applied [teruma oil], the Israelite son of his daughter may rub against it, etc.: The explanation is: a priest who applied teruma oil to himself, his Israelite daughter’s son may come and roll in it; and even if he is an adult and rubs himself against his mother’s father, he need not be concerned. Evidently, once it has been used up in a permitted way, it is used up. And so it is taught explicitly in the Tosefta of tractate Terumot (10:10): A priest applied teruma oil to himself, and he brings his Israelite daughter’s son and rolls him over himself. And it mentions the Israelite son of his daughter because he is regularly with him; the same applies to others.
rashi:a8.1: As he does not bring a provisional guilt offering: for a provisional guilt offering comes only for an uncertain [liability to a] fixed sin offering, as is explained in the last chapter (below, Keritot 25a).
rashi:a10.1: The mishna is referring to one who rejects: Yom Kippur, who said that it should not atone for him. For this reason [the mishna] does not teach it.
rashi:a12.1: And there is a logical inference: that it should not atone.
rashi:a12.2: Only for those who repent: since we require [the offering to be brought] in accordance with his will.
rashi:a13.1: “Guilt offering” is not meant precisely, for we find a guilt offering for an intentional sin in the second chapter (below, Keritot 8b): four [people] bring [an offering] for an intentional [sin].
rashi:a13.2: “Yet”: “Yet on the tenth day of this month it is Yom Kippur.”
rashi:a13.3: Divided: Yom Kippur [atones] for those who repent and not for those who do not repent.
rashi:a14.1: What [is the meaning of] those who repent: that it teaches: they atone only for those who repent.
rashi:a14.2: But it teaches: No, if you said, etc.: and if so, what is it saying? That is the same point.
rashi:a15.1: Rather, like this [statement], etc.: and this is what it is saying: a sin offering atones only for those who repent, who are repentant from the time of designation until the time of sacrifice, and not for one who became an apostate in the interim. And there it wishes to derive [the same for] Yom Kippur: that if he became an apostate before Yom Kippur and retracted after Yom Kippur, another Yom Kippur will no longer atone for him for his transgressions from before his apostasy.
rashi:a16.1: Why? Granted: that with regard to an offering we say that since it was rejected after its designation it is rejected from the altar; but the man, with regard to Yom Kippur, is fit for atonement, like a proper Jew.
rashi:a17.1: And they raise a contradiction: against that which was taught above, that Yom Kippur atones only for those who repent.
rashi:a17.2: Declared it a holy convocation: by arranging the order of prayer.
rashi:a18.1: This is the reading: “It is not difficult: this is Rabbi Yehuda and this is Rabbi.” [Rashi’s text names Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi directly, without “Rabbi in accordance with”.]
rashi:a19.1: Divests the yoke: of all the mitzvot.
rashi:a19.2: Reveals facets: expounds aggadot of scorn, like Manasseh, who would say: Why did Moses need to say, “And Timna was a concubine” [Genesis 36:12]?
rashi:a20.1: The baraita that teaches “Yom Kippur [atones] in any case” is Rabbi.
rashi:a20.2: Rabbi concedes with regard to the transgressions of Yom Kippur: for that which it teaches, “if he did not fast on it,” [means that it] atones for the transgressions of the whole year; but for that transgression of [not] afflicting himself it does not atone. And the “yet,” dividing, that it taught above also speaks of the transgressions of that day itself.
rashi:a20.3: Yom Kippur atones only [during] the day, as it is written (Leviticus 16:30): “For on this day.”
rashi:a20.4: Karet: he goes childless, without children; and if he has [children], they die.
rashi:a22.1: Alternatively, where he performed labor close to sunset: so that there was no time to atone.
rashi:a22.2: Alternatively, as he was performing labor, the hoe with which he was digging cut his thigh and he died: immediately, so that there was no time to atone.
rashi:a23.1: This is the reading: “What is ‘even the blasphemer’?” [Rashi’s text lacks the words “as he does not perform an action”.]
rashi:a24.1: They heard Rabbi Akiva: for the mishna is Rabbi Akiva’s, as is explained below: “The blasphemer brings an offering; this is the statement of Rabbi Akiva.” And they said: Even the blasphemer, too, is like the sorcerer [yidde’oni]. It is puzzling to me: according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said above (3b), “since both of them are stated in a single prohibition,” what is the “even” that is taught in the mishna?
rashi:a25.1: And it states: “Shall bear his sin”: it is explained below that the karet of the blasphemer is speaking of the offering for idol worship.
tosafot:a5.1: Read into it lo yasikh: Even according to one who does not hold that the traditional reading [masoret] is authoritative elsewhere, here it does not add to the word but only rearranges the word, placing a yod between the samekh and the khaf.
tosafot:a6.1: From where with regard to a High Priest who took from the anointing oil, etc.: It is puzzling: why was it not said above that the anointing oil is [a case of] two verses that come as one [and so teach nothing beyond themselves]? One can say that its mitzva is not regarded as completed until the oil has been wiped off, as is concluded: it is called “the anointing oil of his God is upon him”; even though it is upon him, it has not been profaned.
tosafot:a11.1: And in the dispute: That is, just as Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish disagree about one who rejects Yom Kippur, so too Abaye and Rava disagree about one who rejects a sin offering. It does not mean to say that Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish also disagree about one who rejects a sin offering as they do about one who rejects Yom Kippur, for one can say that Reish Lakish said his view only with regard to Yom Kippur, which atones for the intentional as for the unwitting. And if Abaye and Rava also disagreed about Yom Kippur, then when Rava retracted, he would have retracted only with regard to a sin offering, but with regard to Yom Kippur he would not have retracted, and would hold like Reish Lakish and like the other baraita about Yom Kippur, [that it atones] in any case. If so, one halakha would be difficult against another, since we hold like Rabbi Yoḥanan against Reish Lakish and we hold like Rava against Abaye. Rather, it appears that they do not disagree about Yom Kippur. Moreover, we hold like the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi and say that Yom Kippur atones only for those who repent, since the halakha follows Rabbi against his colleague but not against his colleagues. And Rava retracted because of that which is taught, etc.: for one cannot say that he had not heard the baraita, since below he resolves it.
tosafot:a13.1: Shall you say with regard to Yom Kippur, which atones for intentional sins, etc.: It is puzzling: let it say that the four [people] who bring [an offering] for an intentional [sin] will prove [the point], that they atone only for those who repent. And Rivan answered: What [comparison is there] with those, which do not atone for those liable to karet? And [our] teacher said further: Granted that there are sin offerings that atone for the intentional, nevertheless many sin offerings do not atone for the intentional, which is not so with Yom Kippur.
tosafot:a15.1: Since it was rejected, it shall remain rejected: Even though we hold that whatever is in one’s power [to remedy] is not rejection, that applies where it is not rejected because of a disqualification of its own, as when one received the blood and put it into his left hand, which is like having put it on the floor, where he can go back and take it. But this one is rejected because of a disqualification inherent in the person, and it is similar to what we say in Zevaḥim: if the altar was damaged, all the consecrated items that were there are disqualified, even though it is in one’s power to fill in the damage.
tosafot:a17.1: And declared it a holy convocation: that is, with clean clothing, as it says in the Mekhilta: “A holy convocation,” etc.
tosafot:a20.1: And Rabbi concedes with regard to a transgression of the day itself: and this is what the first baraita says, that they do not atone. And the reason it derives the transgressions of the day itself from a sin offering and a guilt offering, which do not atone [without repentance], and does not derive [them] from Yom Kippur itself, which atones without repentance for other transgressions, is that it derives the transgressions of the day, for which Yom Kippur is fixed, from a sin offering and a guilt offering, which are fixed for that very sin, for that is the more reasonable derivation. And one can further say that this is also what it says: “Shall you say with regard to Yom Kippur,” etc., [that is,] instead of deriving it from a sin offering and a guilt offering, derive it from Yom Kippur itself.
tosafot:a22.1: He choked on meat: From here the Riva inferred that with karet one’s offspring are not cut off, since here his offspring did not choke, and Yom Kippur comes and atones for them, and still you do not find karet with regard to his children. And [our] teacher said: Since, while the meat was still between his teeth, the anger of the Lord was kindled against him and He punished him before he found time to obtain atonement, the sin was not forgiven, and his offspring are also cut off; for one cannot say that it was forgiven for them, since they did not sin.
tosafot:a24.1: As it does not involve an action: this is according to Reish Lakish above. But according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, this is what the Rabbis are saying to him: Just as for the Paschal offering and circumcision no offering is brought, since they are [cases of] “sit and do not act,” so too the blasphemer.
gershom:a1.1: [A printer’s marker here reads: “Up to here belongs to 6b.”] The daughter of a priest who married an Israelite: her law is not to eat teruma, and if she ate, she pays the principal but does not pay the fifth, since her law is not that of a complete stranger, for she does eat teruma if she returns, if she becomes a widow or divorcée and has no offspring and returns to her father’s house, etc. And since that is so, her death too is by burning if she commits adultery, according to the law of a priest’s daughter.
gershom:a2.1: She married one of those unfit for her: since she has been profaned, her law is that of a stranger, an Israelite woman.
gershom:a3.1: And the Rabbis say: Both this and that, etc.: that is, since she is not a stranger from her beginning to her end, she does not pay the fifth, and her law is that of a priest’s daughter. And this is [what was meant by]: and they follow their lines of reasoning.
gershom:a4.1: The dispute: concerning that placing of the anointing oil, and according to the answers that we answered: that Rabbi Meir derives from “upon the flesh of a person it shall not be applied” and Rabbi Yehuda derives from giving in general. But with regard to all giving in general, everyone agrees [that it is] with an olive-bulk.
gershom:a5.1: You are saying well, it is written lo yisakh: and you can expound it both as “it shall not be applied” and as “he shall not apply.”
gershom:a6.1: A priest who applied teruma oil: his Israelite daughter’s son, who is not permitted to apply it, nevertheless rolls in it: that Israelite daughter’s son turns over in that oil so as to anoint his whole body, and he need not be concerned about a prohibition, since he did not put it on himself beforehand in a prohibited way.
gershom:a7.1: He said to him: It is not comparable. There, with teruma oil, [it is written] “They will die through it if they profane it”: the priest who applied it is the one punished for having profaned it, and once he has profaned it, it has gone out to non-sacred status; therefore [the grandson] rolls in it without concern. Here, even though it is upon him, it is not profaned, for his head was anointed in a permitted way; and since it is not profaned, when he applies it to his stomach he is liable.
gershom:a8.1: From what does it exclude it? For it teaches “except,” but is he not also liable to karet for the intentional [act] and to a sin offering for the unwitting one? For a sliding-scale offering is a sin offering. This “except” that it teaches is to exclude [one who defiles] the Temple and its consecrated items, in a case where it is unknown to him, from a provisional guilt offering; for one whose sin offering is fixed brings a provisional guilt offering, but not one who brings a sliding-scale offering. If so, since it teaches “except” to exclude from a provisional guilt offering, let it also teach [the exclusion of] one over whom Yom Kippur passed after that uncertain sin offering came into his hands, who does not bring a provisional guilt offering, because Yom Kippur atoned for him.
gershom:a9.1: Reish Lakish said: When it teaches “except,” [it means] a case where his uncertain sin is there and the Merciful One exempts him from a provisional guilt offering, because his sin offering is not fixed. But one over whom Yom Kippur passed has no sin remaining; therefore it is not taught.
gershom:a10.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: This is the reason it does not teach “except for one over whom Yom Kippur passed”: [it speaks] of one who rejects Yom Kippur, who says that Yom Kippur should not atone for him. For if he retracts after Yom Kippur and needs to bring an offering, he is obligated to bring a provisional guilt offering, since Yom Kippur did not atone for him, as he rejected it. And since one who rejects is obligated to bring a provisional guilt offering, it is therefore not taught.
gershom:a11.1: And Reish Lakish holds: [even] apart from my reason, one who rejects is also exempt, for [Yom Kippur] atoned for him.
gershom:a12.1: And in the dispute: Abaye is like Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rava is like Reish Lakish.
gershom:a13.1: Shall you say with regard to Yom Kippur, which atones for the intentional as for the unwitting: as it is written: “And confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel” [Leviticus 16:21].
gershom:a14.1: If you say that those who repent are the unwitting and those who do not repent are the intentional, who did not turn back from his knowledge — but it teaches: No, if you said with regard to a sin offering and a guilt offering, which do not atone for the intentional as for the unwitting; that is the same thing, and what is it answering him?
gershom:a15.1: Rather: what are those who do not repent, for whom it does not atone, since it is written “yet,” dividing? Like that which Ulla said: He ate forbidden fat and designated an offering, and became an apostate before he sacrificed it, and afterward retracted in repentance: since his offering was rejected, as one who did not turn back from his knowledge when he became an apostate, it shall remain rejected. And this is [the meaning of] those who do not repent: one who became an apostate, for whom his offering does not atone.
gershom:a16.1: And he objects: Why call him one who does not repent? Granted that his offering was rejected, since he became an apostate; but since he retracted, the man is fit for atonement.
gershom:a17.1: Rather: is it not that those who repent are one who says “Let my sin offering atone for me,” and those who do not repent are one who rejects, who says “My sin offering should not atone for me,” and it says “yet,” dividing? Evidently Rava retracted, because of what is taught.
gershom:a18.1: And they raise a contradiction: unlike that which is taught, that they do not atone for those who do not repent.
gershom:a19.1: And declared it a holy convocation: with blessings and prayers.
gershom:a21.1: An unattributed Sifra is Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:a22.1: That: which teaches “for it is Yom Kippur,” in any case, is Rabbi according to his own view.
gershom:a23.1: And Rabbi concedes with regard to the transgressions of Yom Kippur itself: and that is [why] it teaches “yet,” dividing.
gershom:a24.1: For if you do not say so: that it does not atone for the transgressions of the day itself, then karet, according to Rabbi, for a transgression of Yom Kippur itself, how can you find it?
gershom:a25.1: And what is the difficulty? On account of this there is no problem, for perhaps one finds karet on Yom Kippur in such a case: where he performed labor the whole night, etc.
gershom:a26.1: That works out well for karet at night: you find it as you said.
gershom:a27.1: Karet for daytime: what is the difficulty? Perhaps, etc. Rather, it is clear as was said at first: this is Rabbi according to Rabbi Yehuda, and that is Rabbi according to his own view.
gershom:a28.1: And the Rabbis say: Even the blasphemer: one does not bring a sin offering for his unwitting [transgression].
gershom:a29.1: Why does it teach “even the blasphemer, which involves no action”? What was being discussed above, that it says “even the blasphemer”? [The printed text is corrected here to read “even”.]
gershom:a30.1: The Rabbis heard Rabbi Akiva, who taught the necromancer and did not teach the sorcerer, etc. And “and it states: shall bear his sin”: it is explained below why they cited it.
rashi:b1.1: We arrive at the Rabbis: [A parenthetical gloss in the printed Rashi reads: “The Rabbis are saying to him; the reading written in the books does not fit the course of the Talmud, and so it appears to me.”] And this is what the Rabbis are saying to Rabbi Akiva: You said that the blasphemer brings an offering, since karet is stated with regard to him in the place of an offering. Do you think that the blasphemer [megaddef] of the verse is one who blesses [i.e., curses] the Name? The blasphemer is one who worships idols. And that which is taught in the mishna, “And the Rabbis say: Even the blasphemer,” etc., this is what they are saying: even your blasphemer, even one who blesses the Name, whom you call a blasphemer [brings no offering].
rashi:b2.1: [This Rashi entry is empty in the source.]
rashi:b2.2: But karet for one who blesses the Name, from where do they [derive it]? With regard to one who blesses the Name it is written: “Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin” (Leviticus 24:15), and it is stated with regard to the Paschal offering (Numbers 9:13): “That man shall bear his sin.” Just as there it is karet, so too here it is karet. And so too there is one who expounds it this way in Pesaḥim, in the chapter Mi SheHaya Tamei (Pesaḥim 93b), and they expound thus: “And refrains from performing the Pesaḥ” is the first [Pesaḥ]; “because he did not bring the offering of the Lord in its appointed time, he shall bear his sin” [is also the first]. And [so] the karet of the blasphemer was not stated in the place of an offering, and we derive it only from the karet of the Paschal offering, which is not subject to a sin offering, since it is a positive mitzva. And Rabbi Akiva holds that there is karet for the second [Pesaḥ], and he applies “shall bear his sin” to the second Pesaḥ and derives it from the blasphemer, and he holds that the blasphemer is one who blesses the Name. And in Pesaḥim (ibid.) too there is one who expounds it this way.
rashi:b4.1: Geirafta: the resh is interchangeable with the dalet [so giddef, “blaspheme,” is like geiref, “scrape clean”]. You emptied the bowl of the cooked food and you also diminished the wood [of the bowl]. He holds that the blasphemer is one who blesses [i.e., curses] the Name, and he has done a grave thing, for he stretched out his hand against the Fundamental [i.e., God].
rashi:b5.1: And did not diminish: he holds that this is one who worships idols, for example, one who sings and plays music for idol worship, which is not so grave a matter.
rashi:b8.1: Mishna. Like a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal or a bird: the reason is explained in tractate Nidda, in the chapter HaMappelet (Nidda 22b): since “forming” is stated with regard to it, as with a person.
rashi:b9.1: A sandal: it is a fetus, but its form has been spoiled.
rashi:b9.2: A placenta: we also say in tractate Nidda, in the chapter HaMappelet (Nidda 26a): there is no placenta without a fetus. And an amniotic sac in which tissue developed: the skin of the fetus, developed, so that inside the sac there is the form of small limbs; it is explained in tractate Nidda, in the chapter HaMappelet.
rashi:b9.3: And likewise a maidservant: a Canaanite one; and in the Gemara it asks why [the mishna] needs to teach it.
rashi:b10.1: And does not know what she miscarried: whether it had a human form, so that she is liable, or [was like] fish and grasshoppers, so that she is exempt.
rashi:b10.2: Bring an offering: two turtledoves, [one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering]. With regard to the burnt offering she stipulates: If I gave birth to a type that obligates, let it be for my obligation, and if not, let it be a voluntary burnt offering. But with regard to the sin offering she cannot stipulate, since there is no voluntary sin offering. And she is obligated [to bring it] in a case of uncertainty, and it is not eaten, since perhaps she is not subject to an offering, and its melika [killing by pinching the neck] would be like that of a mere carcass. And as for [bringing] non-sacred [birds] onto the altar, we are not concerned, since only its blood goes to the altar, and that is not considered eating. And in tractate Nazir (29a) we derive that a bird sin offering may come for an uncertainty.
rashi:b10.3: And likewise two women who miscarried: in a hidden place.
rashi:b10.4: One of a type that exempts: fish and grasshoppers.
rashi:b10.5: And one of a type that obligates: a sandal or a placenta, and it is not known which one miscarried the exempting type and which one the obligating type. Each one brings two turtledoves, as I explained, and it is not eaten.
rashi:b10.6: When: is it not eaten? When they went, etc., for they cannot stipulate, since they brought their nests [pairs of birds] to the priest and went on their way.
rashi:b10.7: But if both of them were standing, etc.: the Gemara explains what they do.
rashi:b11.2: (Like fish and grasshoppers.) [A heading only, with no comment.]
rashi:b11.3: One who miscarries on the fortieth day: in tractate Nidda, in the chapter HaMappelet (Nidda 30a): until forty days of pregnancy have passed, it is mere water.
rashi:b12.1: Gemara. And a maidservant, from where do we [derive it]? As the Sages taught: “Speak to the children of Israel … if a woman conceives.”
rashi:b13.1: What is [the need for] “and likewise a maidservant”? It is obvious to us that in every mitzva in which a woman is obligated a slave is obligated, as we derive it from [the word] “to her”: it is written with regard to a woman (Deuteronomy 24:1), “and he shall write her [lah] a bill of divorce,” and it is written with regard to a maidservant, “nor was freedom given to her [lah]” [Leviticus 19:20].
rashi:b14.1: What do they do? According to Rabbi Yosei, the two of them bring one offering between them: they acquire one bird sin offering jointly. A definite bird burnt offering each one brings definitely, on condition that if she is not obligated it shall be a voluntary offering. But of the bird sin offering she cannot say, “Let it be voluntary,” since there is no voluntary sin offering. Therefore they bring a bird sin offering, acquire it jointly and stipulate: If I am obligated, let your share be forgone to me, and if you are obligated, let my share be forgone to you. And either way, its melika is valid.
rashi:b15.1: Rabbi Shimon says, etc.: in the chapter Dam Sheḥita below (Keritot 23a).
rashi:b16.1: Rabbi Yosei concedes: [with regard to] our mishna, in the chapter Arba’a Meḥusarei Kappara, where they do not bring the offering as a sin offering [for a sin] but to become permitted to eat consecrated food.
rashi:b17.1: There: regarding a sin offering for forbidden fat, in the chapter Dam Sheḥita, the man requires awareness, that he know that he sinned; and if not, each one brings a provisional guilt offering, and not a sin offering in partnership.
rashi:b18.1: As it teaches in the latter clause of that one: in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (ibid.): “Any sin offering that comes for a sin.” Evidently it specifies precisely “that comes for a sin.”
rashi:b19.1: “But if she bears a girl”: it should have written: “But if it is a girl.”
rashi:b21.1: Mishna. On the night of the eighty-first: one who had given birth to a girl miscarried on the night of the eighty-first, when she was fit to bring her atonement offering the next day.
rashi:b21.2: Beit Shammai exempt her from the offering: for the second birth. Even though it is after the completion [of her days], since it is night, she did not emerge into a time fit for an offering, for the night is lacking the time for an offering, as it is written (Leviticus 7:38): “On the day that He commanded.” Therefore, with regard to the offering, it is as though it were within the completion [of her days].
rashi:b22.1: What is different between the night of the eighty-first and the day of the eighty-first: for [if she miscarries on the day] she is certainly obligated, as is explained below in the chapter Arba’a Meḥusarei Kappara (Keritot 9a).
rashi:b22.2: If they are equal with regard to impurity: for you concede that from sunset of the eightieth day her days of purity have ended, and if she saw [blood] on the night of the eighty-first she is impure.
rashi:b26.1: And the blood: of which you say, “If they are equal with regard to impurity,” etc., does not prove [anything] for the offering, for one who miscarries within the completion [of her days], her blood is impure because of the birth, and she is not obligated to bring a second offering.
tosafot:b1.1: Since karet is stated in the place of an offering: It is puzzling: let him derive that he brings [an offering] just as for the other karet transgressions in the Torah, since Rabbi Akiva does not require an action, and all the more so according to Reish Lakish, who holds that a minor action [suffices]. And [our] teacher says: Rabbi Yoḥanan answers according to his own reasoning, that from here Rabbi Akiva derives for the whole Torah that we do not require an action, as with the blasphemer, who is liable. And Reish Lakish answers according to his reasoning, that from here he derives that a minor action suffices.
tosafot:b2.1: Here we arrive at the Rabbis: that is, Rabbi Akiva answered the Rabbis, as it goes on to explain, that [the verse] would not be needed for karet alone, since that is derived by verbal analogy from the Paschal offering.
tosafot:b5.1: The blasphemer is one who worships idols: Rashi explained: one who sings and plays music for idol worship. And it is difficult: why did he explain it so? If because it involves no action, let him say, for example, that he accepted it as a god, saying to it: You are my god. Rather, it appears that the blasphemer is one who worships idols by slaughtering and burning incense, and that is the karet written with regard to idol worship; and they disagree only about one who blesses the Name.
tosafot:b5.2: You cleaned it and diminished it: that is, he did not finish it entirely. Did not diminish it: that is, you did not leave anything lacking but finished it entirely; that is to say, he stretched out his hand against the Fundamental, in that he worshipped idols.
tosafot:b13.1: Say a maidservant is not obligated: It is puzzling: [why not say that] indeed this is so, and the verse is needed for a convert woman? For we say in the Sifrei with regard to the priestly blessing: wherever it speaks of Israel, one needs [a verse] to include the converts.
tosafot:b15.1: Both bring one sin offering: It is puzzling, since it requires leaning [semikha], and both cannot lean on it, for one of them would be performing labor with a consecrated animal.
tosafot:b19.1: Caesarean section [yotzei dofen]: that is, by means of a drug they opened her abdomen and took out the fetus. And Rabbi Y. Levi explained that it came out by way of the rectum. And this does not appear correct, from what is said in the first chapter of Bekhorot regarding a non-kosher fish that swallowed a kosher fish, for example, where it was found in the rectum: conclude from it that it is impossible [for something] to exit by way of the rectum unless it was swallowed and entered through the esophagus, but what is spawned within the innards does not exit by way of the rectum.
tosafot:b19.2: “She bears,” to include: for it is a restriction after a restriction, for “and gives birth” and “she bears” [each] imply: and not a caesarean section.
gershom:b1.1: [A printer’s marker here reads: “Up to here belongs to 7a.”] Karet in the place of an offering: in the passage “And if you err” [Numbers 15:22], which speaks of offerings.
gershom:b2.1: And it states: “Shall bear his sin”: which is written regarding the Paschal offering, for which karet is written: “But the man who is pure and was not on a journey,” etc. [Numbers 9:13]. Here we arrive at the Rabbis: for according to the Rabbis, the second Pesaḥ is derived [through] “his sin” and “his sin” from one who blesses the Name, for karet, as is said below.
gershom:b3.1: And thus Rabbi Akiva said to them, to the Rabbis: You said that the blasphemer involves no action and the karet did not come [to teach] that there is an offering. However, you concede to me that the blasphemer is one who blesses the Name, and that for this reason there is no offering for it, since you hold that the twisting of his lips is no action at all; while according to me, even so he is liable to an offering. But according to you, why is karet written regarding the blasphemer?
gershom:b4.1: They say [to him]: To give karet to one who blesses the Name, who is the blasphemer, and to derive from it karet for the second Pesaḥ. For it is written here, regarding one who blesses, “he shall bear his sin,” and there is karet for it, and it is written regarding the second Pesaḥ, “he shall bear his sin.” Just as there, with one who blesses, it is karet, so too here, with the second Pesaḥ, it is karet; even though karet is written regarding the Paschal offering, as it is written: “But the man who is pure and was not on a journey.”
gershom:b5.1:
The Rabbis hold like Rabbi, according to the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Natan stated in tractate Pesaḥim, in the chapter Mi SheHaya Tamei: [One is] liable for the first and liable for the second; this is the statement of Rabbi. Rabbi Natan says: Liable for the first and exempt for the second. And both derive it from this verse: “But the man who is pure” [Numbers 9:13]. Rabbi holds: “and refrains from performing the Pesaḥ” refers to the first, “and [that soul] shall be cut off”; alternatively, “because he did not bring the offering of the Lord in its appointed time” refers to the second, “he shall bear his sin,” which is karet, derived from “and shall bear his sin” of one who blesses [the Name], who is the blasphemer. And Rabbi Natan holds: “and refrains from performing the Pesaḥ, that soul shall be cut off,” for “he did not bring the offering of the Lord in its appointed time” refers to the first. And what does he do with this “shall bear his sin”? He holds that the blasphemer is not one who blesses the Name but one who sings before idols, and he derives “and shall bear his sin” of one who blesses from “shall bear his sin” of the Paschal offering: just as “his sin” of the Paschal offering is karet, so too “his sin” of one who blesses is karet. And Rabbi Akiva derives karet for one who blesses from “his sin” of the Paschal offering, like Rabbi Natan; [so] the karet of the blasphemer is left over for [teaching] an offering.
Another version: Granted, according to me, for this reason karet is written regarding the blasphemer in the place of an offering: to make him liable to an offering even though it involves no action, and the blasphemer is an apostate for idol worship. But according to you, who say that the blasphemer involves no action and is exempt from an offering, why is karet written regarding the blasphemer? They said to him: To give karet to one who blesses the Name. He said to them: If so, according to you, the blasphemer is not the apostate; then what is the blasphemer itself? They said: It is one who blesses the Name, and we derive from it also karet for the second Pesaḥ, as was said above. And Rabbi Akiva derives karet for one who blesses from the Paschal offering, like Rabbi Natan.
gershom:b6.1: The blasphemer is explained: like one who scrapes a bowl and diminishes the bowl itself: he holds that the blasphemer is one who blesses the Name, that is to say, who stretches out his hand and denies the Fundamental. One who scrapes the bowl and does not diminish it: he holds that the blasphemer is one who worships idols, who sings for idolatry: he scraped the bowl, in that he denied the Fundamental, but did not diminish it, in that he did not stretch out his hand against the holy Name.
gershom:b7.1: One who miscarries [a form] like a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal or a bird: since “forming” is stated with regard to them as with a person.
gershom:b8.1: One who miscarries a sandal: a fetus whose form was spoiled. And an amniotic sac in which tissue developed: as is said in tractate Nidda: the beginning of its formation is from its head, its two eyes like two drops of a fly.
gershom:b9.1: Or a placenta: for there is no placenta without a fetus, but it dissolved.
gershom:b10.1: And one that emerged cut: which the midwife brought out limb by limb.
gershom:b11.1: What is “and likewise a maidservant”? It is obvious, for she has been included [by the verse].
gershom:b12.1: This applies to a matter that is the same for a man and a woman: such as a positive mitzva that is not time-bound.
gershom:b13.1: And does not know what she miscarried: whether she miscarried a fetus or miscarried wind.
gershom:b14.1: One of a type that exempts: like those it mentions afterward, an amniotic sac full of water, etc.; and it is not known which one gave birth to the exempting type.
gershom:b15.1: They bring: it is not eaten, but is to be burned or buried.
gershom:b16.1: Rabbi Yosei said: When is it not eaten? When they went, this one to the east and that one to the west, so that they cannot stipulate. But if both of them were standing here, they bring an offering and it is eaten, for they stipulate: each one says to her fellow, If I miscarried the exempting type and you the obligating type, let my share be given to you. Therefore they bring it and it is eaten.
gershom:b17.1: One offering, a definite one: one offering they bring definitely, for a burnt offering, without a stipulation, because a burnt offering is merely a gift.
gershom:b18.1: And the bird sin offering, which is eaten by the priests, they bring in uncertainty and stipulate.
gershom:b19.1: And is Rabbi Yosei of the opinion that a stipulation [is effective]? But we learned in this tractate, in the chapter Dam Sheḥita, regarding a piece of forbidden fat and a piece of non-sacred [fat]: Rabbi Shimon says: The two of them bring a sin offering, etc.
gershom:b20.1: Rabbi Yosei concedes with regard to one who lacks atonement: as in our mishna about a woman after childbirth, who is one who lacks atonement, that they bring and stipulate.
gershom:b21.1: What is the reason there? With a piece of forbidden fat and a piece of non-sacred fat, what is Rabbi Yosei’s reason that they do not bring one sin offering? For there awareness is required, etc.
gershom:b22.1: As it teaches in the latter clause of that mishna, in Dam Sheḥita: Rabbi Yosei says: Any sin offering, etc.
gershom:b24.1: One who miscarries on the fortieth day: of her pregnancy, for the fetus is formed only at the end of forty-one days.
gershom:b25.1: And a caesarean section: for example, where the walls of the womb were cut open and then it emerged.
gershom:b26.1: “She bears” is superfluous, to include another birth.
gershom:b27.1: From the place where she receives seed: through the womb itself.
gershom:b28.1: On the night of the eighty-first: it speaks of the days of purity of a woman who gave birth to a girl.
gershom:b29.1: Beit Shammai exempt her from a second offering, for they hold: since she did not miscarry at a time fit for bringing the offering for the first birth, she is exempted by the first offering.
gershom:b30.1: And Beit Hillel deem her liable: as they explain the reason: If the night of the eighty-first is equal to the eighty-first day with regard to impurity, for according to everyone she must count other days of impurity and days of purity, shall the night not be equal to the day also to make her liable to a second offering?
gershom:b31.1: Let the one that occurs on Shabbat prove it: for she did not emerge at a time fit to bring an offering, since an individual’s offering does not override Shabbat, and [yet] she is liable to the offering.
gershom:b32.1: The blood, of which you say, “If they are equal with regard to impurity,” does not prove it, for one who miscarries within the completion [of her days], her blood is impure, as she must complete the days of impurity of a miscarriage after the eightieth [day], and she is exempt from the offering, since she miscarried within the completion.
